abstract: Estimates of genetic diversity and effective population size are critical for predicting the resilience of natural populations to environmental change. We generated the first estimates of genetic diversity, effective population size and genomic inbreeding in a wild population of yellow-bellied marmots (Marmota flaviventer) studied continuously in western Colorado since 1962. Using 21 years of data from 284 individuals genotyped at 153,550 minimally filtered SNPs, including 17,393 neutral and unlinked SNPs, we found cryptic patterns of genetic subdivision and migration along a latitudinal gradient. A geographic cline in ancestry revealed a narrow (~900 m) genetic contact zone consistent with limited, unidirectional gene flow from south to north on the landscape. We also discovered a recent, severe decline in both census size and Ne following the winter of 2010 from which the population has yet to recover, contrasting prior trends of demographic expansion over the past century. Genomic inbreeding has remained elevated since this population decline, although long runs of homozygosity remain low in frequency despite pedigreed mating between relatives. Higher maternal inbreeding was associated with lower seasonal mass gain in offspring, consistent with intergenerational inbreeding depression in a trait predictive of annual survival. These findings indicate that while this well-monitored population has persisted at a low Ne with relatively high inbreeding, a recent, indeterminate census collapse and evidence for inbreeding depression in a key fitness-linked trait may threaten its future persistence.
